# London’s blue plaques

London’s famous blue plaques link the people of the past with the buildings of the present. Now run by English Heritage, the London blue plaques scheme was started in 1866 and is thought to be the oldest of its kind in the world.

More than 1,000 plaques across the capital, on buildings humble and grand, honour the notable women and men who have lived or worked in them. Discover some of the people commemorated with blue plaques, or search for a plaque, below.

The English Heritage London blue plaques scheme is generously supported by David Pearl and members of the public.

## New Plaques in 2026

Blue plaques in 2026 will celebrate individuals whose lives and work helped shape London’s intellectual, cultural and social landscape.

Recipients include [Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/01f32b7b5f7a4abba01519ad3212f1af.aspx "Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin"), whose groundbreaking discoveries transformed our understanding of the stars; [Laurence Olivier](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/8d696424a4af488eb20ae3767cab350f.aspx "Laurence Olivier plaque"), whose stage and screen performances defined modern acting; and [Kamal Chunchie](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/35553f686ac045e49ea7470918583496.aspx "Kamal Chunchie"), a tireless advocate for racial equality and community cohesion.

Recently unveiled blue plaques have celebrated people whose creative achievements helped shape the capital, including poet and broadcaster [Una Marson](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/2e89b73942c74f5ea40a4cb91b0be696.aspx "Una Marson"), actress [Audrey Hepburn](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/fa56ecd02b71474c8457cac084363afb.aspx "Audrey Hepburn"), and musician [Marc Bolan](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/c2d8912fe73b46f182c665276a78da0b.aspx "Marc Bolan").

## Plaques for women

Only 15 per cent of London’s blue plaques [celebrate women](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/ca422ae2aaf842dfb870f2bf30b3c87e.aspx "pioneering women"). We don't think that’s good enough, but the picture is improving. Since 2016, when we first launched our ‘plaques for women’ campaign, more than half of the people awarded plaques have been women.Nominations are the life blood of the London blue plaques scheme. If you know of a woman who deserves a blue plaque and meets the [selection criteria](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/bf859faacf324f16bb1e748c20e7c409.aspx), nominate her now.

## Living with disability

We commemorate people from all walks of life, some of whom lived with disability. For some, their disability was a difficulty to be navigated, often in a hostile environment. For others, it changed the course of their lives, and was in some cases central to the achievement for which they're celebrated.

We explore stories of people with both visible and hidden impairments, and consider the impact disability had on their lives.

[Read the article](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/blue-plaque-stories/living-with-disability/)

## Heroes of Health

Advances in the control, treatment and cure of illness and disease have depended on the work of many talented individuals. The London blue plaques scheme celebrates figures of outstanding achievement in this area. We explore their significant medical breakthroughs and public health reforms.

[Read the article](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/blue-plaque-stories/heroes-of-health/)

# London’s blue plaques

London’s famous blue plaques link the people of the past with the buildings of the present. Now run by English Heritage, the London blue plaques scheme was started in 1866 and is thought to be the oldest of its kind in the world.

More than 1,000 plaques across the capital, on buildings humble and grand, honour the notable women and men who have lived or worked in them. Discover some of the people commemorated with blue plaques, or search for a plaque, below.

The English Heritage London blue plaques scheme is generously supported by David Pearl and members of the public.

## New Plaques in 2026

Blue plaques in 2026 will celebrate individuals whose lives and work helped shape London’s intellectual, cultural and social landscape.

Recipients include [Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/01f32b7b5f7a4abba01519ad3212f1af.aspx "Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin"), whose groundbreaking discoveries transformed our understanding of the stars; [Laurence Olivier](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/8d696424a4af488eb20ae3767cab350f.aspx "Laurence Olivier plaque"), whose stage and screen performances defined modern acting; and [Kamal Chunchie](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/35553f686ac045e49ea7470918583496.aspx "Kamal Chunchie"), a tireless advocate for racial equality and community cohesion.

Recently unveiled blue plaques have celebrated people whose creative achievements helped shape the capital, including poet and broadcaster [Una Marson](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/2e89b73942c74f5ea40a4cb91b0be696.aspx "Una Marson"), actress [Audrey Hepburn](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/fa56ecd02b71474c8457cac084363afb.aspx "Audrey Hepburn"), and musician [Marc Bolan](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/c2d8912fe73b46f182c665276a78da0b.aspx "Marc Bolan").

## Plaques for women

Only 15 per cent of London’s blue plaques [celebrate women](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/ca422ae2aaf842dfb870f2bf30b3c87e.aspx "pioneering women"). We don't think that’s good enough, but the picture is improving. Since 2016, when we first launched our ‘plaques for women’ campaign, more than half of the people awarded plaques have been women.Nominations are the life blood of the London blue plaques scheme. If you know of a woman who deserves a blue plaque and meets the [selection criteria](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/link/bf859faacf324f16bb1e748c20e7c409.aspx), nominate her now.

## Living with disability

We commemorate people from all walks of life, some of whom lived with disability. For some, their disability was a difficulty to be navigated, often in a hostile environment. For others, it changed the course of their lives, and was in some cases central to the achievement for which they're celebrated.

We explore stories of people with both visible and hidden impairments, and consider the impact disability had on their lives.

[Read the article](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/blue-plaques/blue-plaque-stories/living-with-disability/)

**Jessica Stewart Dismorr** (3 March 1885 – 29 August 1939) was an English painter and illustrator. Dismorr participated in almost all of the avant-garde groups active in London between 1912 and 1937 and was one of the few English painters of the 1930s to work in a completely abstract manner. She was one of only two women members of the [Vorticist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticism "Vorticism") movement and also exhibited with the [Allied Artists Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_Artists_Association "Allied Artists Association"), the [Seven and Five Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_and_Five_Society "Seven and Five Society") and the [London Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Group "London Group"). She was the only female contributor to [Group X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_X "Group X") and displayed abstract works at the 1937 [Artists' International Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists'_International_Association "Artists' International Association") exhibition. Poems and illustrations by Dismorr appeared in several avant-garde publications including _[Blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blast\_(British\_magazine) "Blast (British magazine)")_, _Rhythm_ and an edition of _Axis_.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Dismorr was born at [Gravesend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravesend,_Kent "Gravesend, Kent") in [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent"), the fourth of five daughters born to Mary Ann Dismorr, née Clowes, and John Stewart Dismorr, a rich businessman with property interests in South Africa, Canada and Australia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) The family moved to [Hampstead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead "Hampstead") in the 1890s, where Jessica Dismorr was educated at Kingsley College and where she became head girl.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) Her mother suffered from extended periods of ill health but her father's income meant the family were free of financial worries and Jessica was able to travel extensively in Europe.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2)

Dismorr attended the [Slade School of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slade_School_of_Art "Slade School of Art") from 1902 to 1903, before training under [Max Bohm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Bohm "Max Bohm") at Etaples in 1904, and at the [Académie de La Palette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_de_La_Palette "Académie de La Palette") in Paris, between 1910 and 1913, where she studied under [Jean Metzinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Metzinger "Jean Metzinger") and was in the circle around the [Scottish Colourist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Colourists "Scottish Colourists"), [John Duncan Fergusson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Duncan_Fergusson "John Duncan Fergusson").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-AFoster-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Pioneer-5) In Paris, Dismorr shared a studio with the American artist [Marguerite Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_Thompson "Marguerite Thompson").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) In 1911, Dismorr contributed several illustrations to [John Middleton Murry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Middleton_Murry "John Middleton Murry")'s avant-garde _[Rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm\_(literary\_magazine) "Rhythm (literary magazine)")_ magazine.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) During July 1912 she showed three landscapes, to favourable reviews, with the [Allied Artists Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_Artists_Association "Allied Artists Association").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) Dismorr exhibited with Fergusson and [S. J. Peploe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S._J._Peploe "S. J. Peploe") in October 1912 at the Stafford Gallery in London.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) From 1912 to 1914 Dismorr also exhibited at the [Salon d'Automne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon_d'Automne "Salon d'Automne") in Paris.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-MWhybrow-7) In 1912 and 1913, Dismorr exhibited [Fauvist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauvism "Fauvism") influenced work with the Allied Artists Association. The Fauvist influence is said to have resulted from her studies at the [Académie de La Palette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_de_La_Palette "Académie de La Palette").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2)

## Vorticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Vorticism")]

Dismorr met [Wyndham Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis "Wyndham Lewis") in 1913 and by 1914 had become a member of the Rebel Art Centre.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) She maintained a studio in the [Kings Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_Road "Kings Road"), [Chelsea, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea,_London "Chelsea, London"), as well as taking frequent trips to France. Dismorr was a signatory to the Vorticist manifesto published in the first issue of their literary magazine, _[Blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blast\_(British\_magazine) "Blast (British magazine)")_ in 1914,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-PDunford-8) and also contributed illustrations and a written piece, _Monologue_, to the second issue in 1915.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) She shared the group's depiction of the dynamics of the machine and their desire to challenge the public's conservative views on art but little of her work from this period survives.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-AFoster-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-PDunford-8) The four works she contributed to the Vorticist exhibition in 1915 are now thought to be lost, as is the original of _The Engine_ which was reproduced in an edition of _Blast_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) Both the [Victoria and Albert Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_and_Albert_Museum "Victoria and Albert Museum") and the [Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate "Tate") hold one example each of Dismorr's work from this period and the collector [John Quinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quinn_(collector) "John Quinn (collector)") displayed several examples in New York in December 1916.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-9) Dismorr exhibited with the Vorticists again in New York in January 1917 at the Penguin Club.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-10)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Jessica_Dismorr_-_Abstract_composition_1915.jpg/250px-Jessica_Dismorr_-_Abstract_composition_1915.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jessica_Dismorr_-_Abstract_composition_1915.jpg)

Abstract composition ca. 1915

Apart from Dismorr, the only other female member of the Vorticist group was [Helen Saunders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Saunders "Helen Saunders").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Pioneer-5) William Roberts's painting _[The Vorticists at the Restaurant de la Tour Eiffel, Spring 1915](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Vorticists\_at\_the\_Restaurant\_de\_la\_Tour\_Eiffel,\_Spring\_1915 "The Vorticists at the Restaurant de la Tour Eiffel, Spring 1915")_,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-11) from 1961–62, shows the seven males dominating the foreground and the two women behind with Dismorr in the doorway being the furthest away.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) According to [Kate Lechmere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Lechmere "Kate Lechmere"), the financial backer of _Blast_ and the Rebel Art Centre, Dismorr had a difficult relationship with Wyndham Lewis, and was, along with Helen Saunders, one of the "little lapdogs who wanted to be Lewis’s slaves and do everything for him".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) Lechmere claimed that on one occasion Dismorr stripped naked in [Oxford Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Street "Oxford Street") to demonstrate she would do anything Lewis asked of her.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) Dismorr and Wyndham Lewis fell out in 1925 when she refused to purchase some drawings from him when he was short of money but they appeared to have resumed a cordial friendship in 1928 when she did lend him some funds.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) Robin Ody, a close friend and the executor of Dismorr's will (in which all the beneficiaries were women), summed her up as "the Edwardian phenomenon of the new woman". Ody considered that she did not have a physical relationship with Lewis. Lechmere's relationship with Lewis ended bitterly, and she carried out a legal struggle to recover money owed her by him. Lechmere had provided all the funds to pay for the Rebel Art Centre, where the Vorticists first met in 1914—a fact which Lewis had to admit to [Christopher Nevinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Nevinson "Christopher Nevinson") who had not wanted "any of these damned women" in the group.

## World War I

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: World War I")]

During [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") Dismorr served as a nurse in France and then as a bilingual field officer with the [American Friends Service Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Friends_Service_Committee "American Friends Service Committee").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) After the war Dismorr was at the centre of the London avant-garde world, acquainted with both [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot") and [Ezra Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound "Ezra Pound"), with her poems and illustrations being published in various publications.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) During 1919 several poems by Dismorr were published in _[The Little Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Little\_Review "The Little Review")_ but following a highly critical article by [A.Y. Winters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvor_Winters "Yvor Winters") she did not submit any more for publication until the 1930s.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) Early in 1920 Dismorr had a handful of paintings shown, in group shows, at both the [Mansard Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansard_Gallery "Mansard Gallery") and the New Art Salon.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1)

From 1920 until 1924 she appears to have had no settled home and travelled throughout Europe, spending time in Paris, the [Alpes-Maritimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpes-Maritimes "Alpes-Maritimes") and in both London and Folkestone.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) She had a nervous breakdown in 1920 and received medical advice not to paint. Lewis suspected that it was her modern style that was causing the doctors concern, and wrote to her that "the best possible distraction for you would be to paint".

## Later life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Later life")]

In 1924 Dismorr began a series of water colour paintings of music hall performers, a popular subject at the time.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) In 1925 her first solo exhibition was held at the Mayor Gallery in London.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Spalding-12)[R. H. Wilenski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._H._Wilenski "R. H. Wilenski") wrote the introduction to the exhibition cataloue.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) The exhibition included a series of water colours of landscapes painted in France, Italy, Spain, Scotland and England.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) A Fauve type composition, _Pyrenean Town_, was reproduced in reviews of the show and also shown at the [Seven and Five Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_and_Five_Society "Seven and Five Society").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) Caring for her ill mother left Dismorr little time to paint and throughout 1926 she mostly showed previously displayed works.

Both her mother and sister Blanche died in 1926 and Dismorr herself was ill during 1927.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) Dismorr recovered and between 1927 and 1934 exhibited some twenty-six figurative pieces with the [London Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Group "London Group").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) In the early 1930s these included a series of portraits of poets, including [Dylan Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_Thomas "Dylan Thomas"), [Cecil Day Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Day_Lewis "Cecil Day Lewis") and [William Empson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Empson "William Empson").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-AFoster-4)

She exhibited with [Charles Ginner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ginner "Charles Ginner") and [Barbara Hepworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Hepworth "Barbara Hepworth") in the London Group, as well as with [Ivon Hitchens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivon_Hitchens "Ivon Hitchens") and [Ben Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Nicholson "Ben Nicholson") in the Seven and Five Society, having joined both groups in 1926.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Spalding-12) Dismorr showed with the anti-fascist [Artists' International Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists'_International_Association "Artists' International Association") in the early 1930s and again in 1937.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Pioneer-5)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Fifty-13) Dismorr was one of seven British women artists included in the 1936 _Die Olympiade ouder Dictatwar_ exhibition in Amsterdam which aimed to counter the Nazi condemnation of [Modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism "Modernism") and modern art.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Fifty-13)

Dismorr produced several pointillist self-portraits alongside portraits of her mother and female friends.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) One of these was of the artist [Catherine Dawson Giles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Dawson_Giles "Catherine Dawson Giles"), whom Dismorr had known since 1904 when they met in Etaples. The two had also travelled together on painting expeditions in Europe in the 1920s.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) For several years Dismorr had lived at the Giles family home in London and also had a studio at Giles' cottage at [Alfriston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfriston "Alfriston") in Sussex.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-AFoster-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) Throughout her final years, Dismorr continued painting and exhibiting her work, which became completely abstract during the late 1930s. She exhibited with the Association Abstraction-Creation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) She contributed her work, "Related Forms" to _Axis_ magazine in 1937 (no 8: 25).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-14)

Dismorr died by suicide by hanging in London on 29 August 1939, five days before Britain declared war on Germany.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2)

## Later exhibitions and research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Later exhibitions and research")]

A joint exhibition of works by Dismorr and Giles was held in 2000 at the Fine Art Society in London, with a catalogue written by Quentin Stevenson.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3)[Pallant House Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pallant_House_Gallery "Pallant House Gallery") held an exhibition of the works of Dismorr and her contemporaries in early 2020.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-:0-15) The exhibition was curated by the Gallery in partnership with Dr Alicia Foster.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-:0-15)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Pioneer-5)

Catherine Heathcock's (unpublished) PhD thesis contains a complete catalogue of Dismorr's works. The letters between Dismorr and Lewis are now held at [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Jessica Stewart Dismorr** (3 March 1885 – 29 August 1939) was an English painter and illustrator. Dismorr participated in almost all of the avant-garde groups active in London between 1912 and 1937 and was one of the few English painters of the 1930s to work in a completely abstract manner. She was one of only two women members of the [Vorticist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticism "Vorticism") movement and also exhibited with the [Allied Artists Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_Artists_Association "Allied Artists Association"), the [Seven and Five Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_and_Five_Society "Seven and Five Society") and the [London Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Group "London Group"). She was the only female contributor to [Group X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_X "Group X") and displayed abstract works at the 1937 [Artists' International Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists'_International_Association "Artists' International Association") exhibition. Poems and illustrations by Dismorr appeared in several avant-garde publications including _[Blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blast\_(British\_magazine) "Blast (British magazine)")_, _Rhythm_ and an edition of _Axis_.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Dismorr was born at [Gravesend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravesend,_Kent "Gravesend, Kent") in [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent"), the fourth of five daughters born to Mary Ann Dismorr, née Clowes, and John Stewart Dismorr, a rich businessman with property interests in South Africa, Canada and Australia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) The family moved to [Hampstead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead "Hampstead") in the 1890s, where Jessica Dismorr was educated at Kingsley College and where she became head girl.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) Her mother suffered from extended periods of ill health but her father's income meant the family were free of financial worries and Jessica was able to travel extensively in Europe.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2)

Dismorr attended the [Slade School of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slade_School_of_Art "Slade School of Art") from 1902 to 1903, before training under [Max Bohm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Bohm "Max Bohm") at Etaples in 1904, and at the [Académie de La Palette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_de_La_Palette "Académie de La Palette") in Paris, between 1910 and 1913, where she studied under [Jean Metzinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Metzinger "Jean Metzinger") and was in the circle around the [Scottish Colourist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Colourists "Scottish Colourists"), [John Duncan Fergusson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Duncan_Fergusson "John Duncan Fergusson").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-AFoster-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Pioneer-5) In Paris, Dismorr shared a studio with the American artist [Marguerite Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_Thompson "Marguerite Thompson").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) In 1911, Dismorr contributed several illustrations to [John Middleton Murry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Middleton_Murry "John Middleton Murry")'s avant-garde _[Rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm\_(literary\_magazine) "Rhythm (literary magazine)")_ magazine.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) During July 1912 she showed three landscapes, to favourable reviews, with the [Allied Artists Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_Artists_Association "Allied Artists Association").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) Dismorr exhibited with Fergusson and [S. J. Peploe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S._J._Peploe "S. J. Peploe") in October 1912 at the Stafford Gallery in London.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) From 1912 to 1914 Dismorr also exhibited at the [Salon d'Automne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon_d'Automne "Salon d'Automne") in Paris.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-MWhybrow-7) In 1912 and 1913, Dismorr exhibited [Fauvist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauvism "Fauvism") influenced work with the Allied Artists Association. The Fauvist influence is said to have resulted from her studies at the [Académie de La Palette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_de_La_Palette "Académie de La Palette").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2)

## Vorticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Vorticism")]

Dismorr met [Wyndham Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis "Wyndham Lewis") in 1913 and by 1914 had become a member of the Rebel Art Centre.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) She maintained a studio in the [Kings Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_Road "Kings Road"), [Chelsea, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea,_London "Chelsea, London"), as well as taking frequent trips to France. Dismorr was a signatory to the Vorticist manifesto published in the first issue of their literary magazine, _[Blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blast\_(British\_magazine) "Blast (British magazine)")_ in 1914,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-PDunford-8) and also contributed illustrations and a written piece, _Monologue_, to the second issue in 1915.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) She shared the group's depiction of the dynamics of the machine and their desire to challenge the public's conservative views on art but little of her work from this period survives.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-AFoster-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-PDunford-8) The four works she contributed to the Vorticist exhibition in 1915 are now thought to be lost, as is the original of _The Engine_ which was reproduced in an edition of _Blast_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) Both the [Victoria and Albert Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_and_Albert_Museum "Victoria and Albert Museum") and the [Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate "Tate") hold one example each of Dismorr's work from this period and the collector [John Quinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quinn_(collector) "John Quinn (collector)") displayed several examples in New York in December 1916.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-9) Dismorr exhibited with the Vorticists again in New York in January 1917 at the Penguin Club.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-10)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Jessica_Dismorr_-_Abstract_composition_1915.jpg/250px-Jessica_Dismorr_-_Abstract_composition_1915.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jessica_Dismorr_-_Abstract_composition_1915.jpg)

Abstract composition ca. 1915

Apart from Dismorr, the only other female member of the Vorticist group was [Helen Saunders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Saunders "Helen Saunders").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Pioneer-5) William Roberts's painting _[The Vorticists at the Restaurant de la Tour Eiffel, Spring 1915](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Vorticists\_at\_the\_Restaurant\_de\_la\_Tour\_Eiffel,\_Spring\_1915 "The Vorticists at the Restaurant de la Tour Eiffel, Spring 1915")_,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-11) from 1961–62, shows the seven males dominating the foreground and the two women behind with Dismorr in the doorway being the furthest away.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) According to [Kate Lechmere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Lechmere "Kate Lechmere"), the financial backer of _Blast_ and the Rebel Art Centre, Dismorr had a difficult relationship with Wyndham Lewis, and was, along with Helen Saunders, one of the "little lapdogs who wanted to be Lewis’s slaves and do everything for him".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) Lechmere claimed that on one occasion Dismorr stripped naked in [Oxford Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Street "Oxford Street") to demonstrate she would do anything Lewis asked of her.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) Dismorr and Wyndham Lewis fell out in 1925 when she refused to purchase some drawings from him when he was short of money but they appeared to have resumed a cordial friendship in 1928 when she did lend him some funds.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) Robin Ody, a close friend and the executor of Dismorr's will (in which all the beneficiaries were women), summed her up as "the Edwardian phenomenon of the new woman". Ody considered that she did not have a physical relationship with Lewis. Lechmere's relationship with Lewis ended bitterly, and she carried out a legal struggle to recover money owed her by him. Lechmere had provided all the funds to pay for the Rebel Art Centre, where the Vorticists first met in 1914—a fact which Lewis had to admit to [Christopher Nevinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Nevinson "Christopher Nevinson") who had not wanted "any of these damned women" in the group.

## World War I

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: World War I")]

During [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") Dismorr served as a nurse in France and then as a bilingual field officer with the [American Friends Service Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Friends_Service_Committee "American Friends Service Committee").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) After the war Dismorr was at the centre of the London avant-garde world, acquainted with both [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot") and [Ezra Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound "Ezra Pound"), with her poems and illustrations being published in various publications.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) During 1919 several poems by Dismorr were published in _[The Little Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Little\_Review "The Little Review")_ but following a highly critical article by [A.Y. Winters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvor_Winters "Yvor Winters") she did not submit any more for publication until the 1930s.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) Early in 1920 Dismorr had a handful of paintings shown, in group shows, at both the [Mansard Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansard_Gallery "Mansard Gallery") and the New Art Salon.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1)

From 1920 until 1924 she appears to have had no settled home and travelled throughout Europe, spending time in Paris, the [Alpes-Maritimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpes-Maritimes "Alpes-Maritimes") and in both London and Folkestone.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) She had a nervous breakdown in 1920 and received medical advice not to paint. Lewis suspected that it was her modern style that was causing the doctors concern, and wrote to her that "the best possible distraction for you would be to paint".

## Later life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Later life")]

In 1924 Dismorr began a series of water colour paintings of music hall performers, a popular subject at the time.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) In 1925 her first solo exhibition was held at the Mayor Gallery in London.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Spalding-12)[R. H. Wilenski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._H._Wilenski "R. H. Wilenski") wrote the introduction to the exhibition cataloue.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) The exhibition included a series of water colours of landscapes painted in France, Italy, Spain, Scotland and England.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) A Fauve type composition, _Pyrenean Town_, was reproduced in reviews of the show and also shown at the [Seven and Five Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_and_Five_Society "Seven and Five Society").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) Caring for her ill mother left Dismorr little time to paint and throughout 1926 she mostly showed previously displayed works.

Both her mother and sister Blanche died in 1926 and Dismorr herself was ill during 1927.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) Dismorr recovered and between 1927 and 1934 exhibited some twenty-six figurative pieces with the [London Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Group "London Group").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) In the early 1930s these included a series of portraits of poets, including [Dylan Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_Thomas "Dylan Thomas"), [Cecil Day Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Day_Lewis "Cecil Day Lewis") and [William Empson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Empson "William Empson").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-AFoster-4)

She exhibited with [Charles Ginner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ginner "Charles Ginner") and [Barbara Hepworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Hepworth "Barbara Hepworth") in the London Group, as well as with [Ivon Hitchens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivon_Hitchens "Ivon Hitchens") and [Ben Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Nicholson "Ben Nicholson") in the Seven and Five Society, having joined both groups in 1926.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Spalding-12) Dismorr showed with the anti-fascist [Artists' International Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists'_International_Association "Artists' International Association") in the early 1930s and again in 1937.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Pioneer-5)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Fifty-13) Dismorr was one of seven British women artists included in the 1936 _Die Olympiade ouder Dictatwar_ exhibition in Amsterdam which aimed to counter the Nazi condemnation of [Modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism "Modernism") and modern art.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Fifty-13)

Dismorr produced several pointillist self-portraits alongside portraits of her mother and female friends.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3) One of these was of the artist [Catherine Dawson Giles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Dawson_Giles "Catherine Dawson Giles"), whom Dismorr had known since 1904 when they met in Etaples. The two had also travelled together on painting expeditions in Europe in the 1920s.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-QStevenson-1) For several years Dismorr had lived at the Giles family home in London and also had a studio at Giles' cottage at [Alfriston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfriston "Alfriston") in Sussex.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-AFoster-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-CTrent-6) Throughout her final years, Dismorr continued painting and exhibiting her work, which became completely abstract during the late 1930s. She exhibited with the Association Abstraction-Creation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2) She contributed her work, "Related Forms" to _Axis_ magazine in 1937 (no 8: 25).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-14)

Dismorr died by suicide by hanging in London on 29 August 1939, five days before Britain declared war on Germany.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-ODNB56-2)

## Later exhibitions and research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jessica_Dismorr&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Later exhibitions and research")]

A joint exhibition of works by Dismorr and Giles was held in 2000 at the Fine Art Society in London, with a catalogue written by Quentin Stevenson.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-DGaze-3)[Pallant House Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pallant_House_Gallery "Pallant House Gallery") held an exhibition of the works of Dismorr and her contemporaries in early 2020.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-:0-15) The exhibition was curated by the Gallery in partnership with Dr Alicia Foster.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-:0-15)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Dismorr#cite_note-Pioneer-5)

Catherine Heathcock's (unpublished) PhD thesis contains a complete catalogue of Dismorr's works. The letters between Dismorr and Lewis are now held at [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

English painter and writer (1882–1957)

This article is about the Vorticist painter and author. For others of that name, see [Wyndham Lewis (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis_(disambiguation) "Wyndham Lewis (disambiguation)").

**Percy Wyndham Lewis** (18 November 1882 – 7 March 1957) was a [Canadian-born](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians_in_the_United_Kingdom "Canadians in the United Kingdom") British writer, painter and critic. He was a co-founder of the [Vorticist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticist "Vorticist") movement in art and edited _[Blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blast\_(British\_magazine) "Blast (British magazine)")_, the literary magazine of the Vorticists.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-NYTart-1)

Lewis is known for his novels _[Tarr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarr "Tarr")_ (1918) and _[The Apes of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Apes\_of\_God "The Apes of God")_ (1930), short story collection _[The Wild Body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wild\_Body "The Wild Body")_ (1927), and autobiography _[Blasting and Bombardiering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blasting\_and\_Bombardiering "Blasting and Bombardiering")_ (1937).

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

### Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life")]

Percy Wyndham Lewis was born on 18 November 1882, reputedly on his father's yacht off the [Canadian province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_province "Canadian province") of [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-odnb-2) His English mother, Anne Stuart Lewis ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%A9e "Née") Prickett), and American father, Charles Edward Lewis, separated about 1893.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-odnb-2) His mother subsequently returned to England. Lewis was educated in England at [Rugby School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_School "Rugby School")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-3) and then, from 16, the [Slade School of Fine Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slade_School_of_Fine_Art "Slade School of Fine Art"), [University College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_London "University College London"), but left for Paris without finishing his course.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-4) He spent most of the 1900s travelling around Europe and studying art in Paris. Whilst there he attended lectures by [Henri Bergson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Bergson "Henri Bergson") on [process philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Process_philosophy "Process philosophy").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-5)

### Early work and development of Vorticism (1908–1915)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early work and development of Vorticism (1908–1915)")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/9f/Wyndham_Lewis%2C_1912%2C_The_Dancers.jpg/330px-Wyndham_Lewis%2C_1912%2C_The_Dancers.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wyndham_Lewis,_1912,_The_Dancers.jpg)

Wyndham Lewis, 1912, _The Dancers_

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/6/65/Workshop-Lewis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Workshop-Lewis.jpg)

Wyndham Lewis, c.1914–15, _Workshop_ ([Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate "Tate"), London)

In 1908 Lewis moved to [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), England, where he would reside for much of his life. In 1909 he published his first work, accounts of his travels in [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany"), in [Ford Madox Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Madox_Ford "Ford Madox Ford")'s _The English Review_. He was a founding member of the [Camden Town Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_Town_Group "Camden Town Group"), which brought him into close contact with the [Bloomsbury Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomsbury_Group "Bloomsbury Group"), particularly [Roger Fry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fry "Roger Fry") and [Clive Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Bell "Clive Bell"), with whom he soon fell out.

In 1912 he exhibited his work at the second [Post-Impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Impressionism "Post-Impressionism") exhibition: [Cubo-Futurist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubo-Futurism "Cubo-Futurism") illustrations to _[Timon of Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timon\_of\_Athens "Timon of Athens")_ and three major oil paintings. In 1912 he was commissioned to produce a decorative mural, a drop curtain, and more designs for [The Cave of the Golden Calf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cave_of_the_Golden_Calf "The Cave of the Golden Calf"), an [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") nightclub and [cabaret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabaret "Cabaret") on [Heddon Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heddon_Street "Heddon Street").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-odnb-2)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-6)

From 1913 to 1915 Lewis developed the style of geometric [abstraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstraction "Abstraction") for which he is best known today, which his friend [Ezra Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound "Ezra Pound") dubbed "[Vorticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticism "Vorticism")". Lewis sought to combine the strong structure of [Cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism"), which he found was not "alive", with the liveliness of [Futurist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism_(art) "Futurism (art)") art, which lacked structure. The combination was a strikingly dramatic critique of modernity. In his early visual works Lewis may have been influenced by Bergson's [process philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Process_philosophy "Process philosophy"). Though he was later savagely critical of Bergson, he admitted in a letter to Theodore Weiss (19 April 1949) that he "began by embracing his evolutionary system." The German philosopher [Friedrich Nietzsche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Nietzsche "Friedrich Nietzsche") was an equally important influence.

Lewis had a brief tenure at Roger Fry's [Omega Workshops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_Workshops "Omega Workshops"), but left after a quarrel with Fry over a commission to provide wall decorations for the [Daily Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_Mail "Daily Mail")[Ideal Home Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_Home_Exhibition "Ideal Home Exhibition"), which Lewis believed Fry had misappropriated. He and several other Omega artists started a competing workshop called the [Rebel Art Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebel_Art_Centre "Rebel Art Centre"). The Centre operated for only four months, but it gave birth to the Vorticist group and its publication, _[Blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blast\_(British\_magazine) "Blast (British magazine)")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-fluxeuropa-7) In _Blast_ Lewis formally expounded the Vorticist aesthetic in a manifesto, distinguishing it from other avant-garde practices. He also wrote and published a play, _Enemy of the Stars_. It is a proto-absurdist, [Expressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expressionism "Expressionism") drama. The Lewis scholar Melania Terrazas identifies it as a precursor to the plays of [Samuel Beckett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Beckett "Samuel Beckett").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-8)

### World War I (1915–1918)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: World War I (1915–1918)")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Wyndham_Lewis_photo_by_George_Charles_Beresford_1917.jpg/330px-Wyndham_Lewis_photo_by_George_Charles_Beresford_1917.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wyndham_Lewis_photo_by_George_Charles_Beresford_1917.jpg)

Wyndham Lewis, photograph by [George Charles Beresford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Charles_Beresford "George Charles Beresford"), 1917

In 1915 the Vorticists held their only British exhibition before the movement broke up, largely as a result of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"). Lewis himself joined up under the [Derby Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_Scheme "Derby Scheme") in March 1916 just before conscription was brought in. He was assigned to the [Royal Garrison Artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Garrison_Artillery "Royal Garrison Artillery") (RGA) and after training was posted to 183rd Siege Battery, RGA, forming at [Weymouth, Dorset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weymouth,_Dorset "Weymouth, Dorset"), in which he served as a [Bombardier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_(rank) "Bombardier (rank)"). At the second attempt he was accepted as an officer cadet and went to the cadet school at [Trowbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trowbridge "Trowbridge") before his battery deployed overseas. On completing his officer training he was commissioned as a [2nd Lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_lieutenant "Second lieutenant") and in January 1917 was posted to the newly-raised [330th Siege Battery, RGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/330th_Siege_Battery,_Royal_Garrison_Artillery "330th Siege Battery, Royal Garrison Artillery"). 330th Siege Battery embarked on 24 May 1917 for the [Western Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Front_(World_War_I) "Western Front (World War I)"). It served on the Flanders coast and then at [Ypres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ypres "Ypres") during the [Third Ypres offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Passchendaele "Battle of Passchendaele"). Much of Lewis's time was spent in [Forward Observation Posts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery_observer "Artillery observer") looking down at apparently deserted German lines, registering targets and calling down fire from batteries massed around the rim of the [Ypres Salient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ypres_Salient "Ypres Salient"). He wrote vivid accounts of narrow misses and deadly artillery duels, though not all of these can be corroborated.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-10)

After the Third Battle of Ypres Lewis was appointed an official [war artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_artist "War artist") for the [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Canada "Government of Canada") and [British governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom"). For the Canadians he painted _[A Canadian Gun-pit](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wyndham\_Lewis-A\_Canadian\_Gun-pit.jpg "c:File:Wyndham Lewis-A Canadian Gun-pit.jpg")_ (1918) from sketches made on [Vimy Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vimy_Ridge "Vimy Ridge"). For the British he painted one of his best-known works, _[A Battery Shelled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Battery\_Shelled "A Battery Shelled")_ (1919), drawing on his own experience at Ypres.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Must_See-11) Lewis exhibited his war drawings and some other paintings of the war in an exhibition, "Guns", in 1918. Although the Vorticist group broke up after the war, Lewis's patron, [John Quinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quinn_(collector) "John Quinn (collector)"), organised a Vorticist exhibition at the Penguin Club in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1917.

Between 1907 and 1911 Lewis had written what would be his first published novel, _[Tarr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarr "Tarr")_, which was revised and expanded in 1914–15[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-12) and serialised in the London literary magazine _[The Egoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Egoist\_(periodical) "The Egoist (periodical)")_ from April 1916 to November 1917. It was first published in book form in 1918 by [Alfred A. Knopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_A._Knopf "Alfred A. Knopf") in New York and by _The Egoist_ in London. It is widely regarded as one of the key texts in [literary modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_modernism "Literary modernism").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-13)

Lewis later documented his experiences and opinions of this period of his life in the autobiographical _Blasting and Bombardiering_ (1937), which covered the time up to 1926.

### _Tyros_ and writing (1918–1929)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tyros and writing (1918–1929)")]

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/6/69/LewisAsTheTyro.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LewisAsTheTyro.jpg)

_Mr Wyndham Lewis as a Tyro_, self-portrait, 1921

After the war Lewis resumed his career as a painter with a major exhibition, _Tyros and Portraits_, at the [Leicester Galleries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester_Galleries "Leicester Galleries") in 1921. "Tyros" were satirical caricatures intended to comment on the culture of the "new epoch" that succeeded the First World War. _A Reading of [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid "Ovid")_ and _Mr Wyndham Lewis as a Tyro_ are the only surviving oil paintings from this series. Lewis also launched his second magazine, _The Tyro_, of which there were only two issues. The second (1922) contained an important statement of Lewis's visual aesthetic: "Essay on the Objective of Plastic Art in our Time".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-14) It was during the early 1920s that he perfected his incisive draughtsmanship.

By the late 1920s he concentrated on writing. He launched another magazine, _The Enemy_ (1927–1929), largely written by himself and declaring its belligerent critical stance in its title. The magazine and other theoretical and critical works he published from 1926 to 1929 mark a deliberate separation from the avant-garde and his previous associates. He believed that their work failed to show sufficient critical awareness of those ideologies that worked against truly revolutionary change in the West, and therefore became a vehicle for these pernicious ideologies.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] His major theoretical and cultural statement from this period is _The Art of Being Ruled_ (1926).

_Time and Western Man_ (1927) is a cultural and philosophical discussion that includes penetrating critiques of [James Joyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Joyce "James Joyce"), [Gertrude Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrude_Stein "Gertrude Stein") and [Ezra Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound "Ezra Pound") that are still read. Lewis also attacked the [process philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Process_philosophy "Process philosophy") of Bergson, [Samuel Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Alexander "Samuel Alexander"), [Alfred North Whitehead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_North_Whitehead "Alfred North Whitehead") and others. By 1931 he was advocating [the art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_ancient_Egypt "Art of ancient Egypt") of [ancient Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt") as impossible to surpass.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-15)

### Fiction and political writing (1930–1936)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Fiction and political writing (1930–1936)")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Wyndham_Lewis_photo_by_George_Charles_Beresford_1929.jpg/330px-Wyndham_Lewis_photo_by_George_Charles_Beresford_1929.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wyndham_Lewis_photo_by_George_Charles_Beresford_1929.jpg)

Lewis in 1929, photographed by [George Charles Beresford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Charles_Beresford "George Charles Beresford")

In 1930 Lewis published _[The Apes of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Apes\_of\_God "The Apes of God")_, a biting satirical attack on the London literary scene, including a long chapter caricaturing the [Sitwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sitwells "The Sitwells") family. The writer [Richard Aldington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Aldington "Richard Aldington"), however, found it "the greatest piece of _writing_ since _[Ulysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses\_(novel) "Ulysses (novel)")_", by [James Joyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Joyce "James Joyce").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-16) In 1937 Lewis published _The Revenge for Love_, set in the period leading up to the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War") and regarded by many as his best novel.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-17) It is strongly critical of [communist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism "Communism") activity in Spain and presents English intellectual [fellow travellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow_traveller "Fellow traveller") as deluded.

Despite serious illness necessitating several operations, he was very productive as a critic and painter. He produced a book of poems, _One-Way Song_, in 1933, and a revised version of _Enemy of the Stars_. An important book of critical essays also belongs to this period: _Men without Art_ (1934). It grew out of a defence of Lewis's satirical practice in _The Apes of God_ and puts forward a theory of "non-moral", or metaphysical, satire. The book is probably best remembered for one of the first commentaries on [William Faulkner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Faulkner "William Faulkner") and a famous essay on [Ernest Hemingway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Hemingway "Ernest Hemingway").

### Return to painting (1936–1941)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Return to painting (1936–1941)")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/ae/Ezra_Pound_by_Wyndham_Lewis%2C_1919.jpeg/330px-Ezra_Pound_by_Wyndham_Lewis%2C_1919.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ezra_Pound_by_Wyndham_Lewis,_1919.jpeg)

Lewis's [Ezra Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound "Ezra Pound"), 1919. The portrait is lost.

After becoming better known for his writing than his painting in the 1920s and early 1930s, he returned to more concentrated work on visual art, and paintings from the 1930s and 1940s constitute some of his best-known work. The _[Surrender of Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Surrender\_of\_Barcelona "The Surrender of Barcelona")_ (1936–37) makes a significant statement about the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War").[_[how?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] It was included in an exhibition at the Leicester Galleries in 1937 that Lewis hoped would re-establish his reputation as a painter. After the publication in _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ of a letter of support for the exhibition, asking for something from the show to be purchased for the national collection (signed by, among others, [Stephen Spender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Spender "Stephen Spender"), [W. H. Auden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._H._Auden "W. H. Auden"), [Geoffrey Grigson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Grigson "Geoffrey Grigson"), [Rebecca West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_West "Rebecca West"), [Naomi Mitchison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naomi_Mitchison "Naomi Mitchison"), [Henry Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Moore "Henry Moore") and [Eric Gill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Gill "Eric Gill")) the [Tate Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Gallery "Tate Gallery") bought the painting, _Red Scene_. Like others from the exhibition, it shows an influence from [Surrealism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") and [Giorgio de Chirico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_de_Chirico "Giorgio de Chirico")'s [metaphysical painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphysical_painting "Metaphysical painting"). Lewis was highly critical of the ideology of Surrealism, but admired the visual qualities of some Surrealist art.

During this period Lewis also produced many of his most well-known portraits, including pictures of [Edith Sitwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Sitwell "Edith Sitwell") ([1923–1936](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Sitwell_(Lewis) "Edith Sitwell (Lewis)")), [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot") ([1938](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_T._S._Eliot "Portrait of T. S. Eliot") and 1949), and [Ezra Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound_(Lewis) "Ezra Pound (Lewis)") ([1939](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Pound_(Lewis) "Ezra Pound (Lewis)")). His 1938 portrait of Eliot was rejected by the selection committee of the [Royal Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Academy "Royal Academy") for their annual exhibition and caused a furore. [Augustus John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_John "Augustus John") resigned in protest.

### Second World War and North America (1941–1945)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Second World War and North America (1941–1945)")]

Lewis spent the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") in the United States and Canada. In 1941 in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto") he produced a series of [watercolour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watercolor_painting "Watercolor painting") fantasies centred on themes of creation, [crucifixion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucifixion "Crucifixion") and bathing.

He grew to appreciate the [cosmopolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmopolitanism "Cosmopolitanism") and "rootless" nature of the American [melting pot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melting_pot "Melting pot"), declaring that the greatest advantage of being American was to have "turned one's back on race, [caste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caste "Caste"), and all that pertains to the rooted state."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Bridson-18) He praised the contributions of [African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") to American culture, and regarded [Diego Rivera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Rivera "Diego Rivera"), [David Alfaro Siqueiros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Alfaro_Siqueiros "David Alfaro Siqueiros") and [José Clemente Orozco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Clemente_Orozco "José Clemente Orozco") as the "best North American artists," predicting that when "the [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_Mexico "Indigenous peoples of Mexico") culture of Mexico melts into the great American mass to the North, the Indian will probably give it its art."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Bridson-18) He returned to England in 1945.

### Later life and blindness (1945–1951)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Later life and blindness (1945–1951)")]

By 1951 he was completely blinded by a [pituitary tumour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pituitary_adenoma "Pituitary adenoma") that placed pressure on his [optic nerve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optic_nerve "Optic nerve"). It ended his career as a painter, but he continued writing until his death. He published several autobiographical and critical works: _Rude Assignment_ (1950), _Rotting Hill_ (1951), a collection of allegorical short stories about his life in "the capital of a dying empire";[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-20)_The Writer and the Absolute_ (1952), a book of essays on writers including [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell"), [Jean-Paul Sartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_Sartre "Jean-Paul Sartre") and [André Malraux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Malraux "André Malraux"); and the semi-autobiographical novel _Self Condemned_ (1954).

The [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") commissioned Lewis to complete his 1928 work _The Childermass_, which was published as _The Human Age_ and dramatised for the [BBC Third Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Third_Programme "BBC Third Programme") in 1955.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-21) In 1956 the [Tate Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Gallery "Tate Gallery") held a major exhibition of his work, "Wyndham Lewis and Vorticism", in the catalogue to which he declared that "Vorticism, in fact, was what I, personally, did and said at a certain period"—a statement which brought forth a series of "Vortex Pamphlets" from his fellow _Blast_ signatory [William Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roberts_(painter) "William Roberts (painter)").

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

From 1918 to 1921, Lewis lived with [Iris Barry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iris_Barry "Iris Barry"), with whom he had two children.[_[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] He is said to have shown little affection for them.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Froanna-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Froanna2-23)

In 1930, Lewis married Gladys Anne Hoskins (1900–1979), who was affectionately known as Froanna. They lived together for 10 years before marrying, and never had children.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-antipathos-24) Lewis did not tell all of his friends about his marriage, as he was jealous of them meeting her.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Froanna-22) Froanna modelled for some of his work, and characters in his books reflect her.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Froanna-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-antipathos-24)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Percy_Wyndham_Lewis_-_Golders_Green_Crematorium.jpg/330px-Percy_Wyndham_Lewis_-_Golders_Green_Crematorium.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Percy_Wyndham_Lewis_-_Golders_Green_Crematorium.jpg)

Plaque dedicated to Lewis at Golders Green Crematorium

He died in 1957 and was cremated at [Golders Green Crematorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golders_Green_Crematorium "Golders Green Crematorium"). By the time of his death he had written 40 books.

### Political views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Political views")]

In 1931, after a visit to [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), Lewis published _Hitler_, a book presenting [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") as a "man of peace", with members of his party being threatened by communist street violence. His unpopularity among liberals and [anti-fascists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-fascism "Anti-fascism") grew, especially after Hitler came to power in 1933.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Following a second visit to Germany in 1937, Lewis changed his views and began to retract his previous political comments. He recognised the reality of Nazi treatment of Jews after a visit to Berlin in 1937. In 1939 he published an attack on [antisemitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism "Antisemitism") titled _The Jews, Are They Human?_,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-25) which was favourably reviewed in _[The Jewish Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jewish\_Chronicle "The Jewish Chronicle")_. He also published _The Hitler Cult_ (1939), which firmly revoked his earlier support for Hitler.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-26)

Politically, Lewis remained an isolated figure through the 1930s. In _Letter to [Lord Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord\_Byron "Lord Byron")_, [W. H. Auden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._H._Auden "W. H. Auden") called Lewis "that lonely old volcano of the Right." Lewis thought there was what he called a "left-wing orthodoxy" in Britain in the 1930s. He believed it was against Britain's self-interest to ally with the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), "which the newspapers most of us read tell us has slaughtered out-of-hand, only a few years ago, millions of its better fed citizens, as well as its whole imperial family."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-27)

In _Anglosaxony: A League that Works_ (1941), Lewis reflected on his earlier support for [fascism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism"):

> Fascism – once I understood it – left me colder than communism. The latter at least pretended, at the start, to have something to do with helping the helpless and making the world a more decent and sensible place. It does start from the human being and his suffering. Whereas fascism glorifies bloodshed and preaches that man should model himself upon the wolf.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Bridson-18)

His sense that America and Canada lacked a British-type [class structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_structure "Class structure") had increased his opinion of [liberal democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_democracy "Liberal democracy"), and in the same pamphlet he defends liberal democracy's respect for individual freedom against its critics on both the left and right.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Bridson-18) In _America and Cosmic Man_ (1949) Lewis argued that [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt"), the [US president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_president "US president") from 1933 to 1945, had successfully managed to reconcile individual rights with the demands of the state.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-Bridson-18)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wyndham_Lewis&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Legacy")]

In recent years[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] there has been renewed critical and biographical interest in Lewis and his work, and he is now regarded as a major British artist and writer of the twentieth century.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-28) Rugby School hosted an exhibition of his works in November 2007 to commemorate the 50-year anniversary of his death. The [National Portrait Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Portrait_Gallery_(London) "National Portrait Gallery (London)") in London held a major retrospective of his portraits in 2008. Two years later the Fundación Juan March[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-29) (Madrid, Spain), held a large exhibition (_Wyndham Lewis 1882–1957_) featuring a comprehensive collection of Lewis's paintings and drawings. As Tom Lubbock pointed out, it was "the retrospective that Britain has never managed to get together."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-31)

In 2010 [Oxford World's Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_World's_Classics "Oxford World's Classics") published a critical edition of the 1928 text of _Tarr_, edited by Scott W. Klein of [Wake Forest University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Forest_University "Wake Forest University"). The [Nasher Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasher_Museum_of_Art "Nasher Museum of Art") at [Duke University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University "Duke University") held an exhibition entitled "[The Vorticists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticism "Vorticism"): Rebel Artists in London and New York, 1914–18" from 30 September 2010 through 2 January 2011.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-32) The exhibition then travelled to the Peggy Guggenheim Collection, [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice "Venice") (29 January – 15 May 2011: "I Vorticisti: Artisti ribelli a Londra e New York, 1914–1918") and then to [Tate Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Britain "Tate Britain") under the title "The Vorticists: Manifesto for a Modern World" between 14 June and 4 September 2011.

Several readings by Lewis are collected on _The Enemy Speaks_, an [audiobook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audiobook "Audiobook") published in [compact disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc "Compact disc") form in 2007 and featuring extracts from "One Way Song" and _The Apes of God_, as well as radio talks titled "When John Bull Laughs" (1938), "A Crisis of Thought" (1947) and "The Essential Purposes of Art" (1951).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-33)

A [blue plaque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_plaque "Blue plaque") now stands on the house in [Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kensington "Kensington"), London, where Lewis lived, No. 61 Palace Gardens Terrace.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyndham_Lewis#cite_note-34)
