**Frederick Etchells** (14 September 1886 – 16 August 1973) was an [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") artist and architect.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Etchells&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Frederick_Etchells_-_Armistice_Day%2C_Munitions_Centre.jpg/250px-Frederick_Etchells_-_Armistice_Day%2C_Munitions_Centre.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frederick_Etchells_-_Armistice_Day,_Munitions_Centre.jpg)

_Armistice Day, Munitions Centre_ by Frederick Etchells

Etchells was born in [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"). He was educated at the London School of Kensington, now [The Royal College of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Royal_College_of_Art "The Royal College of Art"), where he studied on the Architectural course under [Arthur Beresford Pite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Beresford_Pite "Arthur Beresford Pite") and [William Lethaby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lethaby "William Lethaby").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-1) This brought him into contact with the [Bloomsbury Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomsbury_Group "Bloomsbury Group").

He was a contributor to the [Omega Workshops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_Workshops "Omega Workshops"), but eventually broke with Wyndham Lewis.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-2) This break culminated in the establishment of the Rebel Art Centre and the Rebel Art Movement, somewhat akin to the [Dadaists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dadaists "Dadaists") in Paris. The Rebel Art Movement transformed into the [Vorticists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticists "Vorticists") and several of his illustrations appeared in issues of the associated [literary magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_magazine "Literary magazine")_[BLAST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLAST\_(magazine) "BLAST (magazine)")_. [William Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roberts_(painter) "William Roberts (painter)") painted Etchells holding the copy of _BLAST_ in his "[The Vorticists at the Restaurant de la Tour Eiffel, Spring 1915](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vorticists_at_the_Restaurant_de_la_Tour_Eiffel,_Spring_1915 "The Vorticists at the Restaurant de la Tour Eiffel, Spring 1915")".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-3) Etchells eventually decided he no longer wanted anything to do with the movement.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-4) Unlike many of the others from the Vorticists, he remained acquainted with [Roger Fry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fry "Roger Fry").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-5)

In his architectural practice, Etchells produced some modernist buildings. the most well-known are his designs for 232–4 High Holborn, London (1929–30) for the advertising firm [WS Crawford Ltd.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crawford's_Advertising_Agency "Crawford's Advertising Agency"), a commission he had obtained through his friend [Ashley Havinden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Havinden "Ashley Havinden") (1903–73) who was the company’s art director from 1929. This was the first fully modernist office building in central London. Its clean façade was matched by a modern interior, complete with built-in furniture and stainless steel. Etchells's main responsibility was the façade.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-7)

He gradually moved into architecture after a period of book publication, with the [Haslewood Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haslewood_Press?action=edit&redlink=1 "Haslewood Press (page does not exist)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-8) Later he became a church and [conservation architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_architect "Conservation architect"). He had close associations with [John Betjeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Betjeman "John Betjeman") who wrote his obituary.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-JBobit-9) Betjeman was a tenant in one of Etchells's flats in Mayfair, this was during the period when Betjeman was a journalist with _The Architectural Review_. One of his restorations was [St Andrew's Church, Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Andrew's_Church,_Plymouth "St Andrew's Church, Plymouth"); he also restored [St George's Church, Donnington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George's_Church,_Donnington?action=edit&redlink=1 "St George's Church, Donnington (page does not exist)"), [West Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Sussex "West Sussex") after a fire in 1939,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-Pevsner208%E2%80%93209-10) and [St James's Church, Abinger Common](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Church,_Abinger_Common "St James's Church, Abinger Common"), [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrey "Surrey") in 1950 after bomb damage during World War II.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-Pevsner85-11)

He contributed articles to the journal [_The Studio._](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Studio_(magazine) "The Studio (magazine)"), though often anonymously and to _Artwork_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-12)

He was an active member of the [Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings (SPAB)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPAB "SPAB")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-JBobit-9) and a founding member of the [Georgian Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_Group "Georgian Group").

In the 1930s Etchells purchased a weekend cottage in West Challow then called Holme Lea, a Queen Anne property. He lived there between 1939 and 1944, having moved out of London. During that time he acquired and renovated a second smaller house in West Challow into which he, his wife and daughter moved in 1944.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-14)

He was married to [Hester Margaret Sainsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hester_Sainsbury "Hester Sainsbury")[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-Philip-15) who was a book illustrator, painter and artist known for her performances to music.

### Translating Le Corbusier

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Etchells&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Translating Le Corbusier")]

Etchells's most significant work is his controversial 1927 English translation of [Le Corbusier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Corbusier "Le Corbusier")'s _[Vers une architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vers\_une\_architecture "Vers une architecture")_, which he (erroneously) translated as _[Towards a New Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Towards\_a\_New\_Architecture "Towards a New Architecture")_. Other major errors and omissions include the translation of _volume_ as "mass" and the disappearance of Corbusier's original French introduction (replaced with 12 pages of Etchells's own devising) and a passage in the _maisons en série_ essay.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-16) Etchells later translated Corbusier's _Urbanisme_ as _The City of Tomorrow_.

**Frederick Etchells** (14 September 1886 – 16 August 1973) was an [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") artist and architect.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Etchells&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Frederick_Etchells_-_Armistice_Day%2C_Munitions_Centre.jpg/250px-Frederick_Etchells_-_Armistice_Day%2C_Munitions_Centre.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frederick_Etchells_-_Armistice_Day,_Munitions_Centre.jpg)

_Armistice Day, Munitions Centre_ by Frederick Etchells

Etchells was born in [Newcastle upon Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Newcastle upon Tyne"). He was educated at the London School of Kensington, now [The Royal College of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Royal_College_of_Art "The Royal College of Art"), where he studied on the Architectural course under [Arthur Beresford Pite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Beresford_Pite "Arthur Beresford Pite") and [William Lethaby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lethaby "William Lethaby").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-1) This brought him into contact with the [Bloomsbury Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomsbury_Group "Bloomsbury Group").

He was a contributor to the [Omega Workshops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_Workshops "Omega Workshops"), but eventually broke with Wyndham Lewis.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-2) This break culminated in the establishment of the Rebel Art Centre and the Rebel Art Movement, somewhat akin to the [Dadaists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dadaists "Dadaists") in Paris. The Rebel Art Movement transformed into the [Vorticists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticists "Vorticists") and several of his illustrations appeared in issues of the associated [literary magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_magazine "Literary magazine")_[BLAST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLAST\_(magazine) "BLAST (magazine)")_. [William Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roberts_(painter) "William Roberts (painter)") painted Etchells holding the copy of _BLAST_ in his "[The Vorticists at the Restaurant de la Tour Eiffel, Spring 1915](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vorticists_at_the_Restaurant_de_la_Tour_Eiffel,_Spring_1915 "The Vorticists at the Restaurant de la Tour Eiffel, Spring 1915")".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-3) Etchells eventually decided he no longer wanted anything to do with the movement.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-4) Unlike many of the others from the Vorticists, he remained acquainted with [Roger Fry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fry "Roger Fry").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-5)

In his architectural practice, Etchells produced some modernist buildings. the most well-known are his designs for 232–4 High Holborn, London (1929–30) for the advertising firm [WS Crawford Ltd.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crawford's_Advertising_Agency "Crawford's Advertising Agency"), a commission he had obtained through his friend [Ashley Havinden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Havinden "Ashley Havinden") (1903–73) who was the company’s art director from 1929. This was the first fully modernist office building in central London. Its clean façade was matched by a modern interior, complete with built-in furniture and stainless steel. Etchells's main responsibility was the façade.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-7)

He gradually moved into architecture after a period of book publication, with the [Haslewood Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haslewood_Press?action=edit&redlink=1 "Haslewood Press (page does not exist)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-8) Later he became a church and [conservation architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_architect "Conservation architect"). He had close associations with [John Betjeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Betjeman "John Betjeman") who wrote his obituary.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-JBobit-9) Betjeman was a tenant in one of Etchells's flats in Mayfair, this was during the period when Betjeman was a journalist with _The Architectural Review_. One of his restorations was [St Andrew's Church, Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Andrew's_Church,_Plymouth "St Andrew's Church, Plymouth"); he also restored [St George's Church, Donnington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George's_Church,_Donnington?action=edit&redlink=1 "St George's Church, Donnington (page does not exist)"), [West Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Sussex "West Sussex") after a fire in 1939,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-Pevsner208%E2%80%93209-10) and [St James's Church, Abinger Common](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Church,_Abinger_Common "St James's Church, Abinger Common"), [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrey "Surrey") in 1950 after bomb damage during World War II.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-Pevsner85-11)

He contributed articles to the journal [_The Studio._](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Studio_(magazine) "The Studio (magazine)"), though often anonymously and to _Artwork_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-12)

He was an active member of the [Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings (SPAB)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPAB "SPAB")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-JBobit-9) and a founding member of the [Georgian Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_Group "Georgian Group").

In the 1930s Etchells purchased a weekend cottage in West Challow then called Holme Lea, a Queen Anne property. He lived there between 1939 and 1944, having moved out of London. During that time he acquired and renovated a second smaller house in West Challow into which he, his wife and daughter moved in 1944.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-14)

He was married to [Hester Margaret Sainsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hester_Sainsbury "Hester Sainsbury")[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-Philip-15) who was a book illustrator, painter and artist known for her performances to music.

### Translating Le Corbusier

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Etchells&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Translating Le Corbusier")]

Etchells's most significant work is his controversial 1927 English translation of [Le Corbusier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Corbusier "Le Corbusier")'s _[Vers une architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vers\_une\_architecture "Vers une architecture")_, which he (erroneously) translated as _[Towards a New Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Towards\_a\_New\_Architecture "Towards a New Architecture")_. Other major errors and omissions include the translation of _volume_ as "mass" and the disappearance of Corbusier's original French introduction (replaced with 12 pages of Etchells's own devising) and a passage in the _maisons en série_ essay.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Etchells#cite_note-16) Etchells later translated Corbusier's _Urbanisme_ as _The City of Tomorrow_.

**Cuthbert Hamilton** (1885–1959) was a British artist associated with the [Vorticist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticist "Vorticist") movement and later with [Group X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_X "Group X").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1) He was one of the pioneers of abstract art in Britain.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1)

Cuthbert Hamilton went to the [Slade School of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slade_School_of_Art "Slade School of Art") and was a contemporary of Wyndham Lewis.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1) In 1912 he collaborated with Wyndham Lewis on decorations for the [Cave of the Golden Calf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_the_Golden_Calf "Cave of the Golden Calf") nightclub, and the next year he became part of the [Omega Workshops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_Workshops "Omega Workshops").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1)

In 1913 Wyndham Lewis argued with [Roger Fry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fry "Roger Fry") about a commission at the [Omega Workshops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_Workshops "Omega Workshops"). Hamilton left the workshops with other artists [William Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roberts_(painter) "William Roberts (painter)"), Frederick Etchells, [Edward Wadsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Wadsworth "Edward Wadsworth"), and [Henri Gaudier-Brzeska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Gaudier-Brzeska "Henri Gaudier-Brzeska"). They all supported Wyndham Lewis and united with him in March 1914, when he started the [Rebel Art Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebel_Art_Centre "Rebel Art Centre"). The artists were later on associated with the Vorticist art movement.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Tate_Gallery-2) Hamilton was one of the names signing the Vorticist manifesto and he also contributed material to the first issue of the Vorticist magazine _[Blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLAST\_(magazine) "BLAST (magazine)")_,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1) (illus xviii _Group_).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-3)

He opened the Yeoman Pottery in Kensington in 1915/16.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1) During World War I Hamilton was a Special Constable. After the war ended, he exhibited work with a new group Group X, which had been started by Lewis and [Edward McKnight Kauffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer "Edward McKnight Kauffer") also to be an avant-garde group.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Tate_Gallery-2)

Hamilton married the daughter of a powerful insurance businessman, and in 1920 he closed the Yeoman Pottery, giving up all his artistic work. He did not take part in any art exhibitions for the remainder of his life.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1)

**Cuthbert Hamilton** (1885–1959) was a British artist associated with the [Vorticist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticist "Vorticist") movement and later with [Group X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_X "Group X").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1) He was one of the pioneers of abstract art in Britain.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1)

Cuthbert Hamilton went to the [Slade School of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slade_School_of_Art "Slade School of Art") and was a contemporary of Wyndham Lewis.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1) In 1912 he collaborated with Wyndham Lewis on decorations for the [Cave of the Golden Calf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_the_Golden_Calf "Cave of the Golden Calf") nightclub, and the next year he became part of the [Omega Workshops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_Workshops "Omega Workshops").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1)

In 1913 Wyndham Lewis argued with [Roger Fry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fry "Roger Fry") about a commission at the [Omega Workshops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_Workshops "Omega Workshops"). Hamilton left the workshops with other artists [William Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Roberts_(painter) "William Roberts (painter)"), Frederick Etchells, [Edward Wadsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Wadsworth "Edward Wadsworth"), and [Henri Gaudier-Brzeska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Gaudier-Brzeska "Henri Gaudier-Brzeska"). They all supported Wyndham Lewis and united with him in March 1914, when he started the [Rebel Art Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebel_Art_Centre "Rebel Art Centre"). The artists were later on associated with the Vorticist art movement.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Tate_Gallery-2) Hamilton was one of the names signing the Vorticist manifesto and he also contributed material to the first issue of the Vorticist magazine _[Blast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLAST\_(magazine) "BLAST (magazine)")_,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1) (illus xviii _Group_).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-3)

He opened the Yeoman Pottery in Kensington in 1915/16.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1) During World War I Hamilton was a Special Constable. After the war ended, he exhibited work with a new group Group X, which had been started by Lewis and [Edward McKnight Kauffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_McKnight_Kauffer "Edward McKnight Kauffer") also to be an avant-garde group.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Tate_Gallery-2)

Hamilton married the daughter of a powerful insurance businessman, and in 1920 he closed the Yeoman Pottery, giving up all his artistic work. He did not take part in any art exhibitions for the remainder of his life.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Hamilton#cite_note-Artnet-1)

**Frank Owen Dobson**[CBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBE "CBE")[RA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Academy_of_Arts "Royal Academy of Arts") (18 November 1886 – 22 July 1963) was a British artist and sculptor[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODArt-1) and during his time was considered one of the best sculptors in Europe.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-2) He was a contemporary of [Jacob Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Epstein "Jacob Epstein") and [Henry Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Moore "Henry Moore").

Dobson is now seen as one of the most important British sculptors of the 20th century.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-LAGfd-3)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Dobson was born in central London and grew up in [Clerkenwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clerkenwell "Clerkenwell"). His mother was Alice Mary Owen and his father, who was also named Frank Dobson, was a commercial artist who specialized in bird and flower designs for greeting card companies. The younger Dobson attended school in [Forest Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Gate "Forest Gate") and then in [Harrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow,_London "Harrow, London").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) When his father died in 1900, the fourteen year old Dobson was sent to live with an aunt in Hastings. There he attended evening classes at the [Hastings School of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastings_School_of_Art "Hastings School of Art") and was then trained as an apprentice with Sir [William Reynolds-Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reynolds-Stephens "William Reynolds-Stephens").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-NatA-5) After eighteen months in Reynolds-Stephen's studio, Dobson moved to Devon and then to Cornwall where he lived, for two years, by selling landscape paintings.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Newlyn-6) In 1906 he obtained a scholarship to study at the art institute in [Hospitalfield House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospitalfield_House "Hospitalfield House") in Arbroath and studied there for four years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) From 1910 to 1912 Dobson attended the [City and Guilds of London Art School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_and_Guilds_of_London_Art_School "City and Guilds of London Art School") in [Kennington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennington "Kennington"), after which he returned to Cornwall. In Newlyn, he met [Augustus John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_John "Augustus John") who used his influence and contacts to enable Dobson to stage a one-man show at the [Chenil Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chenil_Gallery "Chenil Gallery") in London in 1914.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) In, or around, 1915 Dobson created his first sculpture, a small piece in wood.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Newlyn-6)

## World War One

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: World War One")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/The_Balloon_Apron_Art.IWMART2001.jpg/250px-The_Balloon_Apron_Art.IWMART2001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Balloon_Apron_Art.IWMART2001.jpg)

_The Balloon Apron_ (1918) (Art.IWM ART2001)

In 1915, during the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), Dobson enlisted in The [Artists Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists_Rifles "Artists Rifles") and served in France from October 1916 as a Lieutenant with the 5th [Border Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Regiment "Border Regiment"). In January 1917 he developed a duodenal ulcer and returned to England. In April 1918 he married Cordelia Clara Tregurtha, whom he had first met in Newlyn. Dobson was formally invalided out of the Army in November 1918 and by then had already submitted several drawings to the [British War Memorials Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_War_Memorials_Committee "British War Memorials Committee") and was commissioned to paint a barrage balloon site on the [Thames estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_estuary "Thames estuary"). The Air Force representatives on the Committee did not approve of the picture and Dobson did not receive any further official commissions.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-IWMfodww1-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-WW1Art-8) Dobson set up a studio in the Tregurtha family home in Newlyn but towards the end of the war he took a studio in [Manresa Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manresa_Road "Manresa Road") in Chelsea and would live there until the start of the Second World War.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Newlyn-6)

## Inter-war years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Inter-war years")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Woman_with_a_Fish_Delapre.jpg/250px-Woman_with_a_Fish_Delapre.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Woman_with_a_Fish_Delapre.jpg)

_Woman and the Fish_ at [Delapré Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delapr%C3%A9_Abbey "Delapré Abbey"), Northampton

Dobson began as a painter, and his early work was influenced by [cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism"), [vorticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticism "Vorticism"), and [futurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism_(art) "Futurism (art)"). After [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), however, he turned increasingly toward sculpture in a more or less [realist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realism_(arts) "Realism (arts)") style. Throughout the 1920s and the early 1930s he built a reputation as an outstanding sculptor and was among the first in Britain to prefer direct carving of the material rather than modelling a [maquette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maquette "Maquette") first.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-YaleDAA-9) The simplified forms and flowing lines of much of his sculptures, particularly his female nudes, showed the influence of African art.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Torso-10)

Throughout the 1920s Dobson focused increasingly on sculpture, exhibited work in several influential exhibitions and played a leading role in a number of artistic groups. He was the only sculptor to take part in the 1920 [Group X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_X "Group X") exhibition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-TATEfod-11) Dobson was a founding member of the London Artists Association and spent three years as President of the [London Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Group "London Group") between 1923 and 1927. He made bronze portraits of several public figures. At the Group X exhibition he exhibited two sculptures and studies of [Ben Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Nicholson "Ben Nicholson") and his bronze head of [H. H. Asquith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._H._Asquith "H. H. Asquith") was shown at the Leicester Galleries in late 1921.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) Other subjects included [Osbert Sitwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osbert_Sitwell "Osbert Sitwell"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-TATEosbsit-12)[Lydia Lopokova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydia_Lopokova "Lydia Lopokova") and [Tallulah Bankhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tallulah_Bankhead "Tallulah Bankhead"). Dobson exhibited at the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") in both 1924 and in 1926, was featured in the 1925 Tri-National Exhibition which visited London, Paris and New York and was also included in the 1926 European artists exhibition that toured America and Canada. In March 1927 he had his first major one-man exhibition when the Leicester Galleries exhibited twenty-three of his sculptures and several bronzes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4)

In 1930 the [Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate "Tate") purchased a larger-than-life sculpture from Dobson and erected it outside the gallery on [Millbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millbank "Millbank"). During the early 1930s Dobson continued to receive portrait commissions, most notably for Sir [Edward Marsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Marsh_(polymath) "Edward Marsh (polymath)") and the actress [Margaret Rawlings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Rawlings "Margaret Rawlings"). Dobson worked in other media including textiles and silver, as well. His silver gilt cup, _Calix Majestatis_, to mark the coronation of [George VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_VI "George VI") and [Queen Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_The_Queen_Mother "Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother") is now in the [Royal Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Collection "Royal Collection").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) During 1933 Dobson fractured his left arm which greatly limited his ability for heavy carving and his last monumental stone carving was to be _Pax_, which was first shown at the London Group in 1935.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## World War Two and later

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: World War Two and later")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/AnEscalator_in_an_Underground_Factory_%281944%29_%28Art.IWM_ART_LD_4142%29.jpg/250px-AnEscalator_in_an_Underground_Factory_%281944%29_%28Art.IWM_ART_LD_4142%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AnEscalator_in_an_Underground_Factory_(1944)_(Art.IWM_ART_LD_4142).jpg)

_An Escalator in an Underground Factory_ (1944) (Art.IWM ART LD 4142)

At the start of World War Two, Dobson and his second wife [Caroline] Mary Bussell, whom he had married in 1931,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-14) moved to Bristol, where a large retrospective of his work was held in March 1940. Dobson lived in the city throughout the [Bristol Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Blitz "Bristol Blitz") and like several other artists painted the ruins of churches destroyed in the bombing.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-MlePort-15) Dobson contacted the [War Artists' Advisory Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Artists'_Advisory_Committee "War Artists' Advisory Committee") and offered his services as both a painter and sculptor.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-IWMfodww2-16) WAAC were reluctant to offer sculpture commissions but eventually did offer Dobson a short-term contract for two portrait busts of Naval personnel. Later WAAC commissioned some paintings, including one of workers arriving for work at a factory that had been relocated to a tunnel.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-WW2Art-17)

Dobson was appointed head of sculpture at the Royal College of Art in 1946, a post he held until his retirement in 1953. For the [Festival of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_Britain "Festival of Britain") site on the South Bank of the Thames in 1951, Dobson created [_London Pride_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Pride_(sculpture) "London Pride (sculpture)"). The sculpture was originally exhibited as a plaster cast but was later, after Dobson died, cast as a bronze and placed in front of the [Royal National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Theatre "Royal National Theatre") in 1987. Among his last commissions were a bronze head of Sir [Thomas Lipton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Lipton "Thomas Lipton") and the zodiac clock on the exterior wall of [Bracken House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracken_House,_London "Bracken House, London") in London.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/London_Pride_sculpture_by_Frank_Dobson%2C_South_Bank.jpg/250px-London_Pride_sculpture_by_Frank_Dobson%2C_South_Bank.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:London_Pride_sculpture_by_Frank_Dobson,_South_Bank.jpg)

[_London Pride_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Pride_(sculpture) "London Pride (sculpture)") outside the [National Theatre, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Theatre,_London "National Theatre, London")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Frank_Dobson_%285492237038%29.jpg/250px-Frank_Dobson_%285492237038%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank_Dobson_(5492237038).jpg)

Frank Dobson blue plaque at 14 [Harley Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harley_Gardens "Harley Gardens"), Chelsea, London

Dobson died in 1963 and his ashes were scattered in the Thames.

In 1995 the art critic [Brian Sewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Sewell "Brian Sewell") recalled the great loss of much of Dobson's work after his death: "After his death, his widow asked me to help her clear the studio at Stamford Bridge, and I was appalled at the destruction that she wrought, smashing to smithereens small clay and terracotta models, tearing fine drawings in red and black chalk, hundreds of them, buring[_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")?_] the fragments in a dustbin, all because the subjects were erotic. I was allowed to save pastel drawings of exotic and rare birds, and watercolours of farmyards and a pastoral life long gone, but for the figures engaged in sexual congress, face to face, head to toe and doggy style as explicit as any by his old friend [Eric Gill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Gill "Eric Gill"), Mrs Dobson would accept no plea that they were beautiful, no argument that they were fired by a quality not to be found in the "pure essence" of the torsos that survive, and like a ferociously implacable angel at the Last Judgment, she bent to the business of destruction."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Smashed-18)

[Frank Dobson Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_Square "Frank Dobson Square") was constructed by London County Council in 1963, the year of Dobson's death to commemorate his life and work. The centrepiece of the square was the _Woman and Fish_ fountain, a sculpture designed and completed by Dobson in 1951.

While Dobson was one of the most esteemed artists of his time, after his death his reputation declined with the move towards [postmodernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodernism "Postmodernism") and [conceptual art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conceptual_art "Conceptual art"). However, in recent years a revival has begun.

**Frank Owen Dobson**[CBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBE "CBE")[RA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Academy_of_Arts "Royal Academy of Arts") (18 November 1886 – 22 July 1963) was a British artist and sculptor[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODArt-1) and during his time was considered one of the best sculptors in Europe.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-2) He was a contemporary of [Jacob Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Epstein "Jacob Epstein") and [Henry Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Moore "Henry Moore").

Dobson is now seen as one of the most important British sculptors of the 20th century.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-LAGfd-3)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Dobson was born in central London and grew up in [Clerkenwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clerkenwell "Clerkenwell"). His mother was Alice Mary Owen and his father, who was also named Frank Dobson, was a commercial artist who specialized in bird and flower designs for greeting card companies. The younger Dobson attended school in [Forest Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Gate "Forest Gate") and then in [Harrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow,_London "Harrow, London").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) When his father died in 1900, the fourteen year old Dobson was sent to live with an aunt in Hastings. There he attended evening classes at the [Hastings School of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastings_School_of_Art "Hastings School of Art") and was then trained as an apprentice with Sir [William Reynolds-Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Reynolds-Stephens "William Reynolds-Stephens").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-NatA-5) After eighteen months in Reynolds-Stephen's studio, Dobson moved to Devon and then to Cornwall where he lived, for two years, by selling landscape paintings.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Newlyn-6) In 1906 he obtained a scholarship to study at the art institute in [Hospitalfield House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospitalfield_House "Hospitalfield House") in Arbroath and studied there for four years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) From 1910 to 1912 Dobson attended the [City and Guilds of London Art School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_and_Guilds_of_London_Art_School "City and Guilds of London Art School") in [Kennington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennington "Kennington"), after which he returned to Cornwall. In Newlyn, he met [Augustus John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_John "Augustus John") who used his influence and contacts to enable Dobson to stage a one-man show at the [Chenil Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chenil_Gallery "Chenil Gallery") in London in 1914.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) In, or around, 1915 Dobson created his first sculpture, a small piece in wood.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Newlyn-6)

## World War One

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: World War One")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/The_Balloon_Apron_Art.IWMART2001.jpg/250px-The_Balloon_Apron_Art.IWMART2001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Balloon_Apron_Art.IWMART2001.jpg)

_The Balloon Apron_ (1918) (Art.IWM ART2001)

In 1915, during the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), Dobson enlisted in The [Artists Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists_Rifles "Artists Rifles") and served in France from October 1916 as a Lieutenant with the 5th [Border Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Regiment "Border Regiment"). In January 1917 he developed a duodenal ulcer and returned to England. In April 1918 he married Cordelia Clara Tregurtha, whom he had first met in Newlyn. Dobson was formally invalided out of the Army in November 1918 and by then had already submitted several drawings to the [British War Memorials Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_War_Memorials_Committee "British War Memorials Committee") and was commissioned to paint a barrage balloon site on the [Thames estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_estuary "Thames estuary"). The Air Force representatives on the Committee did not approve of the picture and Dobson did not receive any further official commissions.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-IWMfodww1-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-WW1Art-8) Dobson set up a studio in the Tregurtha family home in Newlyn but towards the end of the war he took a studio in [Manresa Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manresa_Road "Manresa Road") in Chelsea and would live there until the start of the Second World War.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Newlyn-6)

## Inter-war years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Inter-war years")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Woman_with_a_Fish_Delapre.jpg/250px-Woman_with_a_Fish_Delapre.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Woman_with_a_Fish_Delapre.jpg)

_Woman and the Fish_ at [Delapré Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delapr%C3%A9_Abbey "Delapré Abbey"), Northampton

Dobson began as a painter, and his early work was influenced by [cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism"), [vorticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorticism "Vorticism"), and [futurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism_(art) "Futurism (art)"). After [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), however, he turned increasingly toward sculpture in a more or less [realist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realism_(arts) "Realism (arts)") style. Throughout the 1920s and the early 1930s he built a reputation as an outstanding sculptor and was among the first in Britain to prefer direct carving of the material rather than modelling a [maquette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maquette "Maquette") first.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-YaleDAA-9) The simplified forms and flowing lines of much of his sculptures, particularly his female nudes, showed the influence of African art.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Torso-10)

Throughout the 1920s Dobson focused increasingly on sculpture, exhibited work in several influential exhibitions and played a leading role in a number of artistic groups. He was the only sculptor to take part in the 1920 [Group X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_X "Group X") exhibition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-TATEfod-11) Dobson was a founding member of the London Artists Association and spent three years as President of the [London Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Group "London Group") between 1923 and 1927. He made bronze portraits of several public figures. At the Group X exhibition he exhibited two sculptures and studies of [Ben Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Nicholson "Ben Nicholson") and his bronze head of [H. H. Asquith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._H._Asquith "H. H. Asquith") was shown at the Leicester Galleries in late 1921.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) Other subjects included [Osbert Sitwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osbert_Sitwell "Osbert Sitwell"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-TATEosbsit-12)[Lydia Lopokova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydia_Lopokova "Lydia Lopokova") and [Tallulah Bankhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tallulah_Bankhead "Tallulah Bankhead"). Dobson exhibited at the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") in both 1924 and in 1926, was featured in the 1925 Tri-National Exhibition which visited London, Paris and New York and was also included in the 1926 European artists exhibition that toured America and Canada. In March 1927 he had his first major one-man exhibition when the Leicester Galleries exhibited twenty-three of his sculptures and several bronzes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4)

In 1930 the [Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate "Tate") purchased a larger-than-life sculpture from Dobson and erected it outside the gallery on [Millbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millbank "Millbank"). During the early 1930s Dobson continued to receive portrait commissions, most notably for Sir [Edward Marsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Marsh_(polymath) "Edward Marsh (polymath)") and the actress [Margaret Rawlings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Rawlings "Margaret Rawlings"). Dobson worked in other media including textiles and silver, as well. His silver gilt cup, _Calix Majestatis_, to mark the coronation of [George VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_VI "George VI") and [Queen Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_The_Queen_Mother "Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother") is now in the [Royal Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Collection "Royal Collection").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4) During 1933 Dobson fractured his left arm which greatly limited his ability for heavy carving and his last monumental stone carving was to be _Pax_, which was first shown at the London Group in 1935.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## World War Two and later

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: World War Two and later")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/AnEscalator_in_an_Underground_Factory_%281944%29_%28Art.IWM_ART_LD_4142%29.jpg/250px-AnEscalator_in_an_Underground_Factory_%281944%29_%28Art.IWM_ART_LD_4142%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AnEscalator_in_an_Underground_Factory_(1944)_(Art.IWM_ART_LD_4142).jpg)

_An Escalator in an Underground Factory_ (1944) (Art.IWM ART LD 4142)

At the start of World War Two, Dobson and his second wife [Caroline] Mary Bussell, whom he had married in 1931,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-14) moved to Bristol, where a large retrospective of his work was held in March 1940. Dobson lived in the city throughout the [Bristol Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Blitz "Bristol Blitz") and like several other artists painted the ruins of churches destroyed in the bombing.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-MlePort-15) Dobson contacted the [War Artists' Advisory Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Artists'_Advisory_Committee "War Artists' Advisory Committee") and offered his services as both a painter and sculptor.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-IWMfodww2-16) WAAC were reluctant to offer sculpture commissions but eventually did offer Dobson a short-term contract for two portrait busts of Naval personnel. Later WAAC commissioned some paintings, including one of workers arriving for work at a factory that had been relocated to a tunnel.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-WW2Art-17)

Dobson was appointed head of sculpture at the Royal College of Art in 1946, a post he held until his retirement in 1953. For the [Festival of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_Britain "Festival of Britain") site on the South Bank of the Thames in 1951, Dobson created [_London Pride_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Pride_(sculpture) "London Pride (sculpture)"). The sculpture was originally exhibited as a plaster cast but was later, after Dobson died, cast as a bronze and placed in front of the [Royal National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Theatre "Royal National Theatre") in 1987. Among his last commissions were a bronze head of Sir [Thomas Lipton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Lipton "Thomas Lipton") and the zodiac clock on the exterior wall of [Bracken House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracken_House,_London "Bracken House, London") in London.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-ODNB44-4)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/London_Pride_sculpture_by_Frank_Dobson%2C_South_Bank.jpg/250px-London_Pride_sculpture_by_Frank_Dobson%2C_South_Bank.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:London_Pride_sculpture_by_Frank_Dobson,_South_Bank.jpg)

[_London Pride_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Pride_(sculpture) "London Pride (sculpture)") outside the [National Theatre, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Theatre,_London "National Theatre, London")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Frank_Dobson_%285492237038%29.jpg/250px-Frank_Dobson_%285492237038%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frank_Dobson_(5492237038).jpg)

Frank Dobson blue plaque at 14 [Harley Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harley_Gardens "Harley Gardens"), Chelsea, London

Dobson died in 1963 and his ashes were scattered in the Thames.

In 1995 the art critic [Brian Sewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Sewell "Brian Sewell") recalled the great loss of much of Dobson's work after his death: "After his death, his widow asked me to help her clear the studio at Stamford Bridge, and I was appalled at the destruction that she wrought, smashing to smithereens small clay and terracotta models, tearing fine drawings in red and black chalk, hundreds of them, buring[_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")?_] the fragments in a dustbin, all because the subjects were erotic. I was allowed to save pastel drawings of exotic and rare birds, and watercolours of farmyards and a pastoral life long gone, but for the figures engaged in sexual congress, face to face, head to toe and doggy style as explicit as any by his old friend [Eric Gill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Gill "Eric Gill"), Mrs Dobson would accept no plea that they were beautiful, no argument that they were fired by a quality not to be found in the "pure essence" of the torsos that survive, and like a ferociously implacable angel at the Last Judgment, she bent to the business of destruction."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_(sculptor)#cite_note-Smashed-18)

[Frank Dobson Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson_Square "Frank Dobson Square") was constructed by London County Council in 1963, the year of Dobson's death to commemorate his life and work. The centrepiece of the square was the _Woman and Fish_ fountain, a sculpture designed and completed by Dobson in 1951.

While Dobson was one of the most esteemed artists of his time, after his death his reputation declined with the move towards [postmodernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodernism "Postmodernism") and [conceptual art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conceptual_art "Conceptual art"). However, in recent years a revival has begun.

**Charles Isaac Ginner**[CBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Commander of the Order of the British Empire")[ARA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_Member_of_the_Royal_Academy "Associate Member of the Royal Academy") (4 March 1878 – 6 January 1952)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ginner#cite_note-ODNB-1) was a British painter of landscape and urban subjects. Born in the south of France at [Cannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes "Cannes"), of British parents, in 1910 he settled in London, where he was an associate of [Spencer Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist) "Spencer Gore (artist)") and [Harold Gilman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Gilman "Harold Gilman") and a key member of the [Camden Town Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_Town_Group "Camden Town Group").

## Early years and studies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_Ginner&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early years and studies")]

Charles Isaac Ginner was born on 4 March 1878 in Cannes, the second son of Isaac Benjamin Ginner, a British medical doctor. He had a younger sister, [Ruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_Ginner "Ruby Ginner") (b. 1886; who became the dance teacher Ruby Dyer). He was educated in Cannes at the [Institut Stanislas (Cannes)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_Stanislas_(Cannes)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Institut Stanislas (Cannes) (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut%20Stanislas%20(Cannes) "fr:Institut Stanislas (Cannes)")].

At an early age, Ginner formed the intention of becoming a painter, but his parents disapproved. When he was sixteen, he suffered from [typhoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoid "Typhoid") and double pneumonia and travelled in a tramp steamer around the south Atlantic and the Mediterranean to convalesce; on returning to Cannes, he worked in an engineer's office, and in 1899, at the age of 21, moved to Paris to study architecture.

In 1904, his parents withdrew their opposition to his becoming a painter, and Ginner entered the [Academie Vitti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academie_Vitti "Academie Vitti"), where [Henri Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Jean_Guillaume_Martin "Henri-Jean Guillaume Martin") was teaching but where Ginner worked mostly under [Paul Gervais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gervais_(painter) "Paul Gervais (painter)"), who disapproved of Ginner's use of bright colours. In 1905, Ginner moved to the [Ecole des Beaux Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecole_des_Beaux_Arts "Ecole des Beaux Arts"), but in 1906, after Gervais had left, he returned to Vitti's, where his principal teacher was [Hermenegildo Anglada Camarasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermenegildo_Anglada_Camarasa "Hermenegildo Anglada Camarasa"), who disapproved of Ginner's admiration for [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh").

## Painting career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_Ginner&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Painting career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/London_Bridge_by_Charles_Ginner%2C_1913.JPG/250px-London_Bridge_by_Charles_Ginner%2C_1913.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:London_Bridge_by_Charles_Ginner,_1913.JPG)

_London Bridge_, 1913

In 1908, Ginner left Vitti's and worked on his own in Paris, taking [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh"), [Paul Gauguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gauguin "Paul Gauguin"), and [Paul Cézanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_C%C3%A9zanne "Paul Cézanne") for his guides.[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_]

In 1909, Ginner visited [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"), Argentina, where he held his first one-person show, which helped to introduce post-Impressionism to South America. His oil paintings showed the influence of Van Gogh, with their heavy impasto paint.

In 1910, Ginner went to London, to serve on the Hanging Committee of the [Allied Artists Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_Artists_Association "Allied Artists Association")'s third exhibition. [Harold Gilman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Gilman "Harold Gilman") and [Spencer Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist) "Spencer Gore (artist)") became his friends and persuaded him to settle in London. He lived at first in Battersea, but afterwards in Camden Town, where he was a neighbour of Gilman and Gore and regularly attended the Saturday afternoons at 19 Fitzroy Street, meeting [Robert Bevan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bevan_(artist) "Robert Bevan (artist)"), [John Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Nash_(artist) "John Nash (artist)"), Albert Rothenstein, [C. R. W. Nevinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._R._W._Nevinson "C. R. W. Nevinson"), [Jacob Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Epstein "Jacob Epstein"), Walter Bayes, [Walter Sickert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Sickert "Walter Sickert"), and [Lucien Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Pissarro "Lucien Pissarro"). In 1911, he became a member of the [Camden Town Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_Town_Group "Camden Town Group"); in 1913 of the [London Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Group "London Group"); in 1914 of the [Cumberland Market Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Market_Group "Cumberland Market Group").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ginner#cite_note-Grove-2) In 1914 in the _New Age_ he spelt out the artistic creed known as [New Realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neorealism_(art) "Neorealism (art)"). In the same year he showed jointly with Gilman at the [Goupil Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goupil_Gallery "Goupil Gallery").

During [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), in about 1916, Ginner was called up, serving firstly in the [Royal Army Ordnance Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Army_Ordnance_Corps "Royal Army Ordnance Corps"), secondly in the Intelligence Corps, and lastly for the Canadian War Records, for which he made a painting of a powder-filling factory in Hereford.

In 1919, on Gilman's death, he published an appreciation of the artist in _Art and Letters_. In 1920 he became a member of the [New English Art Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_English_Art_Club "New English Art Club").

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") he was again an Official War Artist, and specialised in painting harbour scenes and bombed buildings in London. In 1942 he became an [Associate of the Royal Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_of_the_Royal_Academy "Associate of the Royal Academy"), where he advocated the admission of younger artists.

In 1950, he was awarded a [CBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire").

Ginner painted buildings in an urban context, as in his painting _Plymouth Pier from The Hoe_. His watercolours are unmistakable, with meticulous detailing of trees and buildings.

The [Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate "Tate") Gallery in London and many other galleries hold his work. The [National Portrait Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Portrait_Gallery,_London "National Portrait Gallery, London"), London, has a typically precise self-portrait.

He died in London on 6 January 1952. The [Arts Council of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_Council_of_Great_Britain "Arts Council of Great Britain") held a touring memorial in 1953-4.

**Charles Isaac Ginner**[CBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Commander of the Order of the British Empire")[ARA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_Member_of_the_Royal_Academy "Associate Member of the Royal Academy") (4 March 1878 – 6 January 1952)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ginner#cite_note-ODNB-1) was a British painter of landscape and urban subjects. Born in the south of France at [Cannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes "Cannes"), of British parents, in 1910 he settled in London, where he was an associate of [Spencer Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist) "Spencer Gore (artist)") and [Harold Gilman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Gilman "Harold Gilman") and a key member of the [Camden Town Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_Town_Group "Camden Town Group").

## Early years and studies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_Ginner&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early years and studies")]

Charles Isaac Ginner was born on 4 March 1878 in Cannes, the second son of Isaac Benjamin Ginner, a British medical doctor. He had a younger sister, [Ruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_Ginner "Ruby Ginner") (b. 1886; who became the dance teacher Ruby Dyer). He was educated in Cannes at the [Institut Stanislas (Cannes)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_Stanislas_(Cannes)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Institut Stanislas (Cannes) (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut%20Stanislas%20(Cannes) "fr:Institut Stanislas (Cannes)")].

At an early age, Ginner formed the intention of becoming a painter, but his parents disapproved. When he was sixteen, he suffered from [typhoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoid "Typhoid") and double pneumonia and travelled in a tramp steamer around the south Atlantic and the Mediterranean to convalesce; on returning to Cannes, he worked in an engineer's office, and in 1899, at the age of 21, moved to Paris to study architecture.

In 1904, his parents withdrew their opposition to his becoming a painter, and Ginner entered the [Academie Vitti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academie_Vitti "Academie Vitti"), where [Henri Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Jean_Guillaume_Martin "Henri-Jean Guillaume Martin") was teaching but where Ginner worked mostly under [Paul Gervais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gervais_(painter) "Paul Gervais (painter)"), who disapproved of Ginner's use of bright colours. In 1905, Ginner moved to the [Ecole des Beaux Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecole_des_Beaux_Arts "Ecole des Beaux Arts"), but in 1906, after Gervais had left, he returned to Vitti's, where his principal teacher was [Hermenegildo Anglada Camarasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermenegildo_Anglada_Camarasa "Hermenegildo Anglada Camarasa"), who disapproved of Ginner's admiration for [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh").

## Painting career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Charles_Ginner&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Painting career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/London_Bridge_by_Charles_Ginner%2C_1913.JPG/250px-London_Bridge_by_Charles_Ginner%2C_1913.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:London_Bridge_by_Charles_Ginner,_1913.JPG)

_London Bridge_, 1913

In 1908, Ginner left Vitti's and worked on his own in Paris, taking [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh"), [Paul Gauguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gauguin "Paul Gauguin"), and [Paul Cézanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_C%C3%A9zanne "Paul Cézanne") for his guides.[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_]

In 1909, Ginner visited [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"), Argentina, where he held his first one-person show, which helped to introduce post-Impressionism to South America. His oil paintings showed the influence of Van Gogh, with their heavy impasto paint.

In 1910, Ginner went to London, to serve on the Hanging Committee of the [Allied Artists Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_Artists_Association "Allied Artists Association")'s third exhibition. [Harold Gilman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Gilman "Harold Gilman") and [Spencer Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Gore_(artist) "Spencer Gore (artist)") became his friends and persuaded him to settle in London. He lived at first in Battersea, but afterwards in Camden Town, where he was a neighbour of Gilman and Gore and regularly attended the Saturday afternoons at 19 Fitzroy Street, meeting [Robert Bevan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bevan_(artist) "Robert Bevan (artist)"), [John Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Nash_(artist) "John Nash (artist)"), Albert Rothenstein, [C. R. W. Nevinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._R._W._Nevinson "C. R. W. Nevinson"), [Jacob Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Epstein "Jacob Epstein"), Walter Bayes, [Walter Sickert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Sickert "Walter Sickert"), and [Lucien Pissarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Pissarro "Lucien Pissarro"). In 1911, he became a member of the [Camden Town Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_Town_Group "Camden Town Group"); in 1913 of the [London Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Group "London Group"); in 1914 of the [Cumberland Market Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Market_Group "Cumberland Market Group").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ginner#cite_note-Grove-2) In 1914 in the _New Age_ he spelt out the artistic creed known as [New Realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neorealism_(art) "Neorealism (art)"). In the same year he showed jointly with Gilman at the [Goupil Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goupil_Gallery "Goupil Gallery").

During [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), in about 1916, Ginner was called up, serving firstly in the [Royal Army Ordnance Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Army_Ordnance_Corps "Royal Army Ordnance Corps"), secondly in the Intelligence Corps, and lastly for the Canadian War Records, for which he made a painting of a powder-filling factory in Hereford.

In 1919, on Gilman's death, he published an appreciation of the artist in _Art and Letters_. In 1920 he became a member of the [New English Art Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_English_Art_Club "New English Art Club").

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") he was again an Official War Artist, and specialised in painting harbour scenes and bombed buildings in London. In 1942 he became an [Associate of the Royal Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_of_the_Royal_Academy "Associate of the Royal Academy"), where he advocated the admission of younger artists.

In 1950, he was awarded a [CBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire").

Ginner painted buildings in an urban context, as in his painting _Plymouth Pier from The Hoe_. His watercolours are unmistakable, with meticulous detailing of trees and buildings.

The [Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate "Tate") Gallery in London and many other galleries hold his work. The [National Portrait Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Portrait_Gallery,_London "National Portrait Gallery, London"), London, has a typically precise self-portrait.

He died in London on 6 January 1952. The [Arts Council of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_Council_of_Great_Britain "Arts Council of Great Britain") held a touring memorial in 1953-4.
